Lesson 2 · Business route

Read patterns without overclaiming

What budget covers a useful share of lodging offers?

The business problem

Finance proposes a single lodging cap of 140 CU for staff travel. The cap should control spend, but it also has to work when an employee books a real trip. A company-wide average is useful for a budget forecast; it tells little about how often a traveler in a particular town will find a suitable offer under the cap. The travel manager therefore frames the question as coverage: what share of relevant quotes would the rule actually allow?

What the data show

Among 360 prices, the sample mean is 123.73 CU and the median is 119.08 CU. The difference points to a right tail: a single typical-price number hides some costly offers.

A mean below the cap can coexist with many exceptions because prices have a high-cost tail. Destination mix also matters. A town with many quotes can dominate the pooled average, while a town with few affordable options creates most of the approval requests. For each destination, count offers at or below 140 and divide by that town’s own quote count. Put those shares beside the distribution of prices and the number of quotes, so the manager sees both typical spend and day-to-day friction.

What would you decide?

Show the share of eligible offers below the proposed budget in each town. Use each town’s quote count as its denominator, then design an exception process for destinations with few options.

Keep the cap as a starting rule and define a fast exception path for destinations with limited compliant offers. Require travelers to record the best eligible offer they found, including room and cancellation requirements, rather than justify a price against the average alone. Over the next quarter, compare exceptions, final paid prices, and the destinations actually visited. That review shows whether the cap saves money without slowing routine bookings.

Pause and explain

Would the overall mean alone be enough to set a travel budget?

Compare your reasoning

No. The tail, the proportion under the budget and the mix of towns matter to the decision.

Check your judgment

Reveal the case’s known answer

The case draws towns with different price distributions. The overall mean therefore changes with the mix of destinations, while town-level coverage shows where the cap will be hardest to use.

The bigger picture

Business policies affect people at the edges of a distribution, not only at its center. A cap can meet an average spending target while creating frequent exceptions for particular destinations. The useful management question is how a rule performs across the work the organization actually does. This idea travels to inventory limits, service targets, credit rules, and staffing plans: show both the overall result and who or what encounters the rule most often. The next lesson asks how large an observed difference needs to be before changing a policy.
